files.Title: Cosmos.Kernel.Core.Scheduler.IScheduler
files.Summary:
A scheduling policy: everything that decides which thread runs when. The mechanism around it (the thread registry, the lifecycle transitions, the timer-tick entry, the register save and restore) is fixed. Install an implementation with .

Every hook runs in the kernel's most sensitive window. Most are called with interrupts already masked, and the two scheduling hooks run inside the timer interrupt itself; each member below says which. No hook may block, park, or wait, and none may allocate on the tick path. Four get no mask from the manager (, and the two run-queue diagnostics) and must take themselves before touching the run structure. The spinlock around is not a substitute: it excludes another caller, not the tick.

Several hooks have no mechanism-side caller yet, because the kernel runs on one CPU and nothing in-tree sets priorities. Implement them, but do not expect them to be exercised.

Two rules hold for every hook. Each must tolerate being called more than once for the same thread, and each must tolerate an empty slot, because clears it and a thread can lose its record between a tick and the hook that observes it; that is why a hook reads the slot with as and never a cast. A record written by a different policy is never handed to a hook: re-homes every live thread through on the outgoing policy and on the incoming one.

Inspired by Ekiben's EkibenScheduler trait.

files.Title: Cosmos.Kernel.Core.Scheduler.InterruptMaskScope
files.Summary: Masks maskable interrupts on the current CPU for the lifetime of the scope and restores the previous interrupt state on dispose. Obtained from ; use it in a using statement around scheduler entry points the manager does not already guard (diagnostics reads, tuning setters), so the timer tick cannot observe a half-mutated run structure.

files.Title: Cosmos.Kernel.Core.Scheduler.PerCpuState
files.Summary: Per-CPU scheduling state.

files.Title: Cosmos.Kernel.Core.Scheduler.SchedulerExtensible
files.Summary: Base class for objects that can hold scheduler-specific extension data.

files.Title: Cosmos.Kernel.Core.Scheduler.SchedulerManager
files.Summary: Manages scheduler lifecycle and dispatches to current scheduler.

files.Title: Cosmos.Kernel.Core.Scheduler.SchedulerThread
files.Summary: Thread Control Block for scheduling. A kernel that only wants to read thread state does not come here: SchedulerDiagnostics on the ring hands out a KernelThreadInfo snapshot of the fields that survive an unlocked read, and reaching this type means acknowledging the seam's diagnostic first.

files.Title: Cosmos.Kernel.Core.Scheduler.SchedulerThreadFlags
files.Summary: Thread flags.

files.Title: Cosmos.Kernel.Core.Scheduler.SchedulerThreadState
files.Summary: Thread execution state.

files.Title: Cosmos.Kernel.HAL.Devices.Audio.AudioBitDepth
files.Summary: Bits per sample in one channel. The value is the channel's size in bytes, so (int)depth is what a stride calculation needs.

files.Title: Cosmos.Kernel.HAL.Devices.Audio.AudioFormat
files.Summary: The layout of one audio frame: how many bits a channel holds, how many channels a frame interleaves, and whether the samples are signed. A format is not a rate: carries that, because the same layout plays at every rate the codec accepts.

files.Title: Cosmos.Kernel.HAL.Devices.Audio.AudioSink
files.Summary: Where an audio driver reports that it drained a buffer or changed format, returned by . Kit-owned; see . Allocation-free; any context, so the driver may report a completion straight from its interrupt handler.

files.Title: Cosmos.Kernel.HAL.Devices.Audio.IAudioOutput
files.Summary: What an audio output driver implements and hands to . The kernel pushes frames in with and the device drains them on its own clock, the mirror of : the driver owns the ring, the caller never blocks on it, and a short write is how the device says it is full. The driver reports the room it frees through . Called by the ring in thread context.

files.Title: Cosmos.Kernel.HAL.Devices.Display.DisplayMode
files.Summary: A display's geometry, pixel format and refresh rate. A mode is not the display's identity: it changes when the canvas switches it.

files.Title: Cosmos.Kernel.HAL.Devices.Display.DisplaySink
files.Summary: Where a display driver reports a mode change, returned by . Kit-owned; see . Allocation-free; any context.

files.Title: Cosmos.Kernel.HAL.Devices.Display.IDisplay
files.Summary: What a display driver implements and hands to . Called by the ring in thread context.

files.Title: Cosmos.Kernel.HAL.Devices.Display.IDisplayModes
files.Summary: A display that can switch modes. Optional facet on an , found by a type test on the published object. Thread context.

files.Title: Cosmos.Kernel.HAL.Devices.Display.IHardwareCursor
files.Summary: A display that composes a cursor itself. Optional facet on an , found by a type test on the published object. Thread context.

files.Title: Cosmos.Kernel.HAL.Devices.Input.IKeyboard
files.Summary: What a keyboard driver implements and hands to . Called by the ring in thread context.

files.Title: Cosmos.Kernel.HAL.Devices.Input.IPointer
files.Summary: What a pointer driver implements and hands to .

files.Title: Cosmos.Kernel.HAL.Devices.Input.KeyboardLeds
files.Summary: Keyboard indicator lights.

files.Title: Cosmos.Kernel.HAL.Devices.Input.KeyboardSink
files.Summary: Where a keyboard driver reports keys, returned by . Kit-owned: it finds the ring's keyboard consumer at call time and drops the report when the device was withdrawn or nobody listens. Allocation-free; any context.

files.Title: Cosmos.Kernel.HAL.Devices.Input.PointerButtons
files.Summary: Pointer buttons, as a set.

files.Title: Cosmos.Kernel.HAL.Devices.Input.PointerSink
files.Summary: Where a pointer driver reports movement, returned by . Kit-owned; see . Allocation-free; any context.

files.Title: Cosmos.Kernel.HAL.Devices.Network.INetworkInterface
files.Summary: What a network driver implements and hands to . Called by the ring in thread context.

files.Title: Cosmos.Kernel.HAL.Devices.Network.MacAddress
files.Summary: A 48-bit Ethernet MAC address.

files.Title: Cosmos.Kernel.HAL.Devices.Network.NetworkSink
files.Summary: Where a network driver reports frames and link changes, returned by . Kit-owned; see . Allocation-free; any context.

files.Title: Cosmos.Kernel.HAL.Devices.Storage.IBlockDevice
files.Summary:
Interface for block storage devices (SATA, NVMe, virtio-blk, etc.). Block-level read/write only; partitioning and filesystems sit above this.

Error contract: , and throw on failure (device error, timeout, out-of-range request). A return without an exception means the operation completed on the device.

files.Title: Cosmos.Kernel.HAL.DriverKit.Buses.Pci.PciAccess
files.Summary: The access object of a PCI node: the function's configuration space, its sized base address registers, its capability list and the Command register bits a driver turns on. Behind it, for the kit only, the bus hooks: the function is quiesced before the first driver sees it (bus mastering off, legacy line disabled, a firmware-enabled MSI-X masked and disabled), quiesced again after each probe that did not bind, before the probe's memory is freed, restored as firmware left it when nobody binds, and quiesced once more after a binding is torn down. A bound driver owns the state from its probe on and enables what it needs. For a bridge it also carries the secondary and subordinate bus and, for a hot-plug slot, the describe of the functions behind it with the kit's one resource assignment. Any context and allocation-free except , which is thread context and allocates the description.

files.Title: Cosmos.Kernel.HAL.DriverKit.Buses.Pci.PciBar
files.Summary: One base address register of a PCI function as the host sized it at describe time: what the slot decodes, where, and how much. The six slots are always reported; the upper half of a 64-bit register and a slot with no register behind it are unassigned with length 0; an implemented register nobody has assigned yet is unassigned with the length its mask decoded, which is what the kit's placement for a function arriving behind a hot-plug slot uses. The resource at the same index on the node is the mappable form.

files.Title: Cosmos.Kernel.HAL.DriverKit.Buses.Pci.PciFunctionDescription
files.Summary: Everything a PCI host or bridge driver publishes for one function, as or read it: the arguments of , in order, and whether the device has functions beyond 0. A default instance, which the describe returns with false, holds nothing.

files.Title: Cosmos.Kernel.HAL.DriverKit.Buses.Pci.PciHostAccess
files.Summary: The access object of a PCI host platform node: the configuration mechanism of one segment's buses (the x86 ports, or an ECAM window the machine description found in MCFG), raw configuration access over it, and , which reads a function's header, sizes its base address registers and builds everything a host driver publishes for it. Created by the machine description through the internal factories; the host driver enumerates with it.

files.Title: Cosmos.Kernel.HAL.DriverKit.Buses.Pci.PciIdentity
files.Summary: The identity of a PCI function as its configuration header states it: where it is (segment, bus, device, function) and what it is (vendor, device, subsystem, class, revision, header layout). Read once by the host that described the function; never changes. Path is pci:ssss:bb:dd.f, all hexadecimal.

files.Title: Cosmos.Kernel.HAL.DriverKit.Buses.Pci.PciMatch
files.Summary: A match over PCI identities: every field given must equal the function's, every field left null is not looked at, and the specificity is the number of fields given. A match that constrains nothing is refused: a catch-all driver would be offered every function on the bus, the ones other drivers want included.

files.Title: Cosmos.Kernel.HAL.DriverKit.Buses.Platform.PlatformIdentity
files.Summary: The identity of a platform device: a root node the machine description publishes because no bus enumerates it, named the way a device tree would name it. is the node's "name" form (pci, pci@3f000000), and the list of strings drivers match on, most specific first. Path is platform:name.

files.Title: Cosmos.Kernel.HAL.DriverKit.Buses.Platform.PlatformMatch
files.Summary: A match over platform identities: one compatible string (specificity 1) or any platform device (specificity 0).

files.Title: Cosmos.Kernel.HAL.DriverKit.Buses.Ps2.Ps2Access
files.Summary: The access object of a Ps2 node, one per port, constructed by the 8042 driver: the byte stream from the port (a receive ring the leaf drains from its handler with ), the command exchange (: the command byte and its arguments each acknowledged by 0xFA, resent on 0xFE, then the reply bytes) and the port's interrupt source, which the access raises for every stream byte. The controller driver hands every byte the status register attributed to the port to , which either completes the step of the exchange in flight or appends the byte to the ring and raises the source. The kit holds the protocol and nothing of the hardware: the controller driver maps the ports and connects the lines. The execution context of each member is in its summary.

files.Title: Cosmos.Kernel.HAL.DriverKit.Buses.Ps2.Ps2Controller
files.Summary: The contract an 8042 controller driver implements for the kit: how a byte is sent to a port, how the status register is polled once, and whether bytes arrive on their own (interrupts or a periodic drain) or only while a probe polls. The controller driver binds the 8042's platform node, owns its two ports and its two lines, and creates one over this object per port; the kit never reaches a port or an interrupt controller for this bus kind. A controller driver implements the protected members; the kit calls them through the internal ones, so a leaf driver holding a reference can reach neither.

files.Title: Cosmos.Kernel.HAL.DriverKit.Buses.Ps2.Ps2Identity
files.Summary: The identity of a Ps2 node: the port of the 8042 it hangs off, and nothing else. Paths are ps2:kbd and ps2:aux. Constructed by the 8042 driver in Cosmos.Kernel.Drivers, so the constructor is public, as 's is.

files.Title: Cosmos.Kernel.HAL.DriverKit.Buses.Ps2.Ps2Match
files.Summary: A match over Ps2 identities: one port, specificity 1. There is no match for any port: the bus has two ports of different kinds, and a driver matching both would be offered a mouse's port as a keyboard.

files.Title: Cosmos.Kernel.HAL.DriverKit.Buses.Ps2.Ps2Port
files.Summary: The two ports of an 8042 keyboard controller. The identity of a Ps2 node is its port and nothing else: the device behind it is identified by the leaf driver, which resets it anyway.

files.Title: Cosmos.Kernel.HAL.DriverKit.Buses.Synthetic.SyntheticAccess
files.Summary: The synthetic bus's access object: the bytes the test attached to the device, and, when a window was asked for, a view of the RAM page behind resource 0, so a test can read what a driver wrote through its and write what the driver will read.

files.Title: Cosmos.Kernel.HAL.DriverKit.Buses.Synthetic.SyntheticBus
files.Summary: A bus with no hardware behind it, for tests: publishes nodes on demand, retracts them, and raises their interrupts. A node may carry a register window backed by one RAM page, so , and the test can see each other's writes without remapping normal memory as device memory.

files.Title: Cosmos.Kernel.HAL.DriverKit.Buses.Synthetic.SyntheticIdentity
files.Summary: The identity of a synthetic device: a key the test chose. Path is synthetic:key.

files.Title: Cosmos.Kernel.HAL.DriverKit.Buses.Synthetic.SyntheticMatch
files.Summary: A match over synthetic identities: one key (specificity 1) or any synthetic device (specificity 0).

files.Title: Cosmos.Kernel.HAL.DriverKit.Buses.Usb.UsbAccess
files.Summary: The access object of a USB interface node, the one thing a class driver sees: the interface's identity and endpoints, control transfers on the device's default pipe (serialized across the device's interfaces), the pipes it opens on the ledger of its binding, bulk transfers through them, and, for a hub driver, the enumeration core for the hub's ports. One per interface node. Every member is thread context unless its summary says otherwise: a probe, a work item, a driver thread or a ring caller, never an interrupt handler; called from one (a on a controller that delivers reports in interrupt context), a member stops with an exception naming itself in a synthetic dispatch, or a panic in a real interrupt, as the binding's members do.

files.Title: Cosmos.Kernel.HAL.DriverKit.Buses.Usb.UsbBus
files.Summary: One USB bus: a bound host controller, its 1-based ordinal, the device tree below it and the enumeration core's entry points for root ports. The host driver creates it from its probe and calls and for root ports from its probe and its hot-plug thread; the hub driver reaches the same core for hub ports through and . The tree is guarded by one IRQ-safe lock around list changes only, never across a transfer or a kit call: the host thread and a hub thread change it concurrently. The execution context of each member is in its summary.

files.Title: Cosmos.Kernel.HAL.DriverKit.Buses.Usb.UsbClassCode
files.Summary: Base class codes a class driver matches an interface against (usb.org "Defined Class Codes").

files.Title: Cosmos.Kernel.HAL.DriverKit.Buses.Usb.UsbDescriptorType
files.Summary: Descriptor types (USB 2.0 section 9.4 table 9-5, hub class section 11.23.2.1, USB 3.2 table 9-6 and section 10.15.2.1).

files.Title: Cosmos.Kernel.HAL.DriverKit.Buses.Usb.UsbDevice
files.Summary: One USB function behind one port: the host created it when it addressed the port (an xHCI slot) and derives from it to carry its per-device state and the transfer primitives; the enumeration core fills the identity it read from the descriptors. A host implements the protected members; the kit calls them through the internal ones, so a class driver holding a reference can reach none of them and goes through its instead.

files.Title: Cosmos.Kernel.HAL.DriverKit.Buses.Usb.UsbEndpoint
files.Summary: One endpoint descriptor of an interface (USB 2.0 section 9.6.6), as the enumeration core parsed it. Any context, immutable after parsing.

files.Title: Cosmos.Kernel.HAL.DriverKit.Buses.Usb.UsbEndpointType
files.Summary: Transfer type of an endpoint, from bmAttributes bits 1:0.

files.Title: Cosmos.Kernel.HAL.DriverKit.Buses.Usb.UsbHostController
files.Summary: The contract a USB host controller driver implements for the kit: how a device on a port gets its address and how its state is freed again. The host driver binds the controller's own node (a PCI function for xHCI), creates a over this object from its probe, and owns every register, ring, context and DMA page; the kit never publishes a node for the controller itself. A host implements the protected members; the kit calls them through the internal ones, so a class driver holding a reference can reach neither.

files.Title: Cosmos.Kernel.HAL.DriverKit.Buses.Usb.UsbHubProtocol
files.Summary: The protocol numbers of the hub class (USB 2.0 chapter 11, USB 3.2 chapter 10), so a hub driver carries numbers, not a copy of the kit's state machine. Constants; any context.

files.Title: Cosmos.Kernel.HAL.DriverKit.Buses.Usb.UsbIdentity
files.Summary: The identity of one interface of a USB device, as the enumeration core read it from the descriptors: where it is (the port path from the host controller down, the interface number), what the device is (vendor, product, device class triplet, speed) and what the interface is (its class triplet). Read once when the device was attached; never changes. Path is usb:<port path>:<interface number>, so a stick on root port 1 of the first controller is usb:1-1:0.

files.Title: Cosmos.Kernel.HAL.DriverKit.Buses.Usb.UsbMatch
files.Summary: A match over USB interface identities: every field given must equal the identity's, every field left null is not looked at, and the specificity is the number of fields given. The port path and the speed are identity, not match fields. A match that constrains nothing is refused. So a vendor and product match (2) outranks a class-only match (1) and a full interface triplet (3) outranks both.

files.Title: Cosmos.Kernel.HAL.DriverKit.Buses.Usb.UsbPipe
files.Summary: An opened endpoint: an interrupt IN pipe that delivers reports to a , or a bulk pipe (IN or OUT) the driver transfers through and . The host creates it and derives its own pipe kinds from it; the kit records it on the ledger of the binding that opened it and closes it in the unwind, or earlier through . Any context for the two getters.

files.Title: Cosmos.Kernel.HAL.DriverKit.Buses.Usb.UsbReportHandler
files.Summary: Receives one completed transfer of an interrupt IN pipe. Interrupt context, under no lock, on a controller with a message interrupt; on a polled one, thread context on whichever thread drains the controller's events (its hot-plug thread, or any thread waiting on one of its commands or transfers), under the host's own ; the span is valid for the call only; the handler must not block, allocate, or call any or member; it may call a sink and , and may use on its own fields.

files.Title: Cosmos.Kernel.HAL.DriverKit.Buses.Usb.UsbRequestType
files.Summary: bmRequestType of a setup packet (USB 2.0 section 9.3.1): one direction, one type and one recipient, OR-ed together.

files.Title: Cosmos.Kernel.HAL.DriverKit.Buses.Usb.UsbSetupPacket
files.Summary: The 8-byte SETUP packet that opens every control transfer (USB 2.0 section 9.3). Any context, immutable.

files.Title: Cosmos.Kernel.HAL.DriverKit.Buses.Usb.UsbSpeed
files.Summary: Bus speed of a USB device. The values are the xHCI default Protocol Speed IDs (xHCI 1.2 section 7.2.2.1.1), which is what a root port reports and what a Slot Context takes; another host controller translates its own numbering to these.

files.Title: Cosmos.Kernel.HAL.DriverKit.Buses.Usb.UsbStandardRequest
files.Summary: Standard request codes (USB 2.0 section 9.4 table 9-4). Hub-class requests reuse the same codes with a class request type (section 11.24.2); requests only one class defines live with that class driver.

files.Title: Cosmos.Kernel.HAL.DriverKit.Buses.Usb.UsbTransferStatus
files.Summary: Outcome of a synchronous USB transfer, independent of the host controller that carried it.

files.Title: Cosmos.Kernel.HAL.DriverKit.Buses.Virtio.VirtioAccess
files.Summary: The access object of a virtio node, the one thing a leaf driver sees: the status handshake, the feature negotiation, the virtqueues and the device configuration space, run once here over whatever the transport driver built. Behind it, for the kit only, the bus hooks: the device is reset and brought to DRIVER state before the first probe and again after a probe that did not bind, left reset when nobody binds, and reset after a binding is torn down. The node's interrupt sources are the access's own nine objects (the configuration change, then one per queue), multiplexed over the transport's entries by . Constructed by a transport driver in Cosmos.Kernel.Drivers, so the constructor is public. The execution context of each member is in its summary.

files.Title: Cosmos.Kernel.HAL.DriverKit.Buses.Virtio.VirtioDeviceType
files.Summary: The device ids of virtio specification section 5, as a transport reads them from the function's device id (PCI) or the DeviceID register (MMIO). The list is not exhaustive: a value outside it is a type the kit has no name for, and prints the number. Any context.

files.Title: Cosmos.Kernel.HAL.DriverKit.Buses.Virtio.VirtioIdentity
files.Summary: The identity of a virtio device as its transport driver published it: which transport carries it, the transport's own address for it, and the device type. The path is virtio:pci:0000:00:03.0 or virtio:mmio:a003e00: the transport is visible in the path and invisible to the leaf driver, which matches on the type alone. Built by a transport driver in Cosmos.Kernel.Drivers, so the constructor is public. Any context.

files.Title: Cosmos.Kernel.HAL.DriverKit.Buses.Virtio.VirtioInterruptStatus
files.Summary: What a virtio device signalled with one interrupt. The bit values are the ISR status bits of the specification (section 4.1.4.5 over PCI, the InterruptStatus register over MMIO), so a transport hands the register through unchanged. Interrupt context; allocation-free.

files.Title: Cosmos.Kernel.HAL.DriverKit.Buses.Virtio.VirtioMatch
files.Summary: A match over virtio identities: one device type (specificity 1) or any virtio device (specificity 0). The transport underneath is never part of a match. Any context.

files.Title: Cosmos.Kernel.HAL.DriverKit.Buses.Virtio.VirtioTransport
files.Summary: What a transport driver implements over its registers so the kit's can run the status handshake, the feature negotiation and the virtqueues once, for every transport. The kit calls these members; a leaf driver never sees the transport, only the access. A transport driver in Cosmos.Kernel.Drivers derives from this, so the constructor is protected and the members are public abstract. The execution context of each member is in its summary.

files.Title: Cosmos.Kernel.HAL.DriverKit.Buses.Virtio.Virtqueue
files.Summary: A split virtqueue (virtio specification section 2.6) over DMA memory the leaf's binding owns, created by . Not thread-safe: the driver serializes its use, with a between its transmit path and its drain. Every member is allocation-free, so a handler may pop used buffers; the members that touch the rings order them with the DMA barriers. Dead once the binding that created it was torn down: every ring member throws from then on, in every build, as does, so a consumer that kept a reference across a withdrawal gets the exception and never a write into freed pages. The kit never rounds a size: queue sizes are powers of two by the specification, and QEMU offers 256 or 1024.

files.Title: Cosmos.Kernel.HAL.DriverKit.Buses.Virtio.VirtqueueDescriptorFlags
files.Summary: The flags of a split virtqueue descriptor (VIRTQ_DESC_F_*, virtio specification section 2.6.5). Any context.

files.Title: Cosmos.Kernel.HAL.DriverKit.Buses.Virtio.VirtqueueLayout
files.Summary: Where the kit placed the three rings of one split virtqueue in physical memory: built by , consumed by a transport's , which programs the addresses (a modern transport) or the page frame number and the alignment (a legacy MMIO transport). Any context.

files.Title: Cosmos.Kernel.HAL.DriverKit.DetachCause
files.Summary: Why a bound device is being taken away from its driver.

files.Title: Cosmos.Kernel.HAL.DriverKit.DetachReason
files.Summary: Handed to : why the device is going away and whether the hardware is still there to be quiesced.

files.Title: Cosmos.Kernel.HAL.DriverKit.DeviceBinding
files.Summary:
A driver's handle on one device, created for each offer and kept while the driver is bound. Everything a driver acquires goes through it and is written to its ledger: windows, regions, DMA memory, interrupts, events, work items, periodic work, threads, USB pipes, published devices, child nodes. When the driver declines, fails, or the device goes away, the kit releases the ledger in a fixed order and the driver frees nothing itself. A is the one thing on the ledger that is nothing to release: it is recorded for the diagnostics only.

Every member here is thread context: probe, work items, driver threads. Called from an interrupt handler, a member stops with an exception naming itself (in a synthetic dispatch) or a panic (in a real interrupt). Once is true no new resource can be acquired.

files.Title: Cosmos.Kernel.HAL.DriverKit.DeviceIdentity
files.Summary: What a bus knows about a device before any driver looks at it: the bus name, a bus-specific address, and a description for the log. Each bus kind derives its own identity type (synthetic, platform, PCI, virtio, USB and PS/2) and the matching types read the fields they constrain.

files.Title: Cosmos.Kernel.HAL.DriverKit.DeviceMatch
files.Summary: One entry of a driver's match table: a predicate over a plus how specific it is. When several drivers match a node, the kit offers the highest priority first, then the most specific match, then the earliest manifest position.

files.Title: Cosmos.Kernel.HAL.DriverKit.DeviceNode
files.Summary: A device a bus found, in the kit's tree: its identity, the resources and interrupt sources it exposes, the bus's own access object, and where it is in its life. A node stays in with its state until it is retracted, when it leaves the list; the object keeps its state, its offers and its last binding for whoever still holds it. Lists a reader may see while the worker changes them are copy-on-write arrays, so a snapshot is always consistent.

files.Title: Cosmos.Kernel.HAL.DriverKit.DeviceOffer
files.Summary: One offer of a node to a driver and how it ended, kept on the node for the diagnostics view: which drivers were tried, in what order, and why each one passed.

files.Title: Cosmos.Kernel.HAL.DriverKit.Driver
files.Summary:
Base class of every driver the kit can bind. A driver declares what it matches, is offered nodes that match, and in either takes a node, acquiring what it needs through the binding, or passes.

The manifest constructs one instance per driver class, and that instance is offered every node it matches, so fields on the driver are shared across bindings: state that belongs to one device lives on objects the driver creates in and hangs off . Probes, teardowns and work items run one at a time on the kit worker; only driver threads run concurrently, with each other and with the worker.

Execution contexts: and run in thread context on the kit worker and may block through the binding. Interrupt handlers requested through the binding run in interrupt context and reach only what the binding says they may.

files.Title: Cosmos.Kernel.HAL.DriverKit.DriverAttribute
files.Summary: Marks a class for the manifest the build generates. The kernel project's manifest registers every marked class it can see, in a fixed order (the kernel's own classes in declaration order, then referenced assemblies by name), subject to the kernel's policy: a CosmosDriverExclude item drops a driver, a CosmosDriverInclude item adds one whose is false, and ties the registration to a feature switch.

files.Title: Cosmos.Kernel.HAL.DriverKit.DriverFeature
files.Summary: A kernel feature switch a driver can be tied to through . The manifest generator registers such a driver only when the matching CosmosEnable* property is on, so a kernel that turns the feature off never carries the driver. The members mirror the properties of Cosmos.Kernel.System.KernelFeatures by name; a host-side test keeps the two lists equal.

files.Title: Cosmos.Kernel.HAL.DriverKit.DriverRegistry
files.Summary: The drivers this kernel carries, in manifest order. The generated manifest fills it before the kernel starts; the engine reads it for every arbitration. Manifest position is the last arbitration key, so the order here is the order drivers are offered a node when priority and specificity tie.

files.Title: Cosmos.Kernel.HAL.DriverKit.Interrupts.InterruptContext
files.Summary: The whole of what an may do besides touching its registers and DMA memory. Every member is allocation-free and never blocks; the handler has no other route to the kit, which is how blocking from interrupt context stays unreachable by type.

files.Title: Cosmos.Kernel.HAL.DriverKit.Interrupts.InterruptHandle
files.Summary: A connected interrupt, returned by . The driver masks and unmasks through it from any context; the kit disconnects it at teardown. A handler that throws leaves its source masked, with the fault recorded on the node; the driver may unmask again.

files.Title: Cosmos.Kernel.HAL.DriverKit.Interrupts.InterruptHandler
files.Summary: A driver's interrupt handler. Runs in interrupt context with interrupts masked on the interrupted stack: it acknowledges the device through a , reads what it must from DMA memory, and hands everything else to a thread through context. It must not allocate, block, or reach the binding.

files.Title: Cosmos.Kernel.HAL.DriverKit.Interrupts.InterruptSource
files.Summary: One interrupt a can deliver: a legacy line, one message of an MSI or MSI-X block, or a synthetic source a test raises. A driver picks one by index from and asks the binding to connect a handler; the source knows how to route it on its platform, and how to mask it at the controller. A bus implements the protected members; the kit calls them through the internal ones, so a driver holding a source can neither connect nor mask it behind the kit's back. Every implementation keeps its connection state under one IRQ-safe lock, so a raise cannot see a half-built connection and a handler never runs after returned.

files.Title: Cosmos.Kernel.HAL.DriverKit.Interrupts.InterruptTrampoline
files.Summary: The kit's dispatcher between an and a driver's . The source calls with interrupts masked; the trampoline enters the interrupt-context guard, runs the handler, and turns an exception into a recorded fault instead of a crash: the fault is counted on the node, the source is masked so a handler that throws once cannot throw on every delivery, and a preallocated work item logs it in thread context. Nothing here allocates: the message kept is the exception's own.

files.Title: Cosmos.Kernel.HAL.DriverKit.NodeState
files.Summary: Where a is in its life.

files.Title: Cosmos.Kernel.HAL.DriverKit.ProbeOutcome
files.Summary: How an offer of a device to a driver ended.

files.Title: Cosmos.Kernel.HAL.DriverKit.ProbeResult
files.Summary: What returns. keeps the binding and everything acquired through it; and make the kit release the binding's ledger in reverse order and record the reason with the offer.

files.Title: Cosmos.Kernel.HAL.DriverKit.Resources.DeviceRegion
files.Summary: A bulk device region mapped through : a framebuffer, a command queue, a descriptor area. Where a checks and orders every access, a region is memory: fills it, copies structs into it, and the driver orders what needs ordering with and . carves a sub-range that goes dead with its parent. The accessors neither allocate nor block.

files.Title: Cosmos.Kernel.HAL.DriverKit.Resources.DeviceResource
files.Summary: One resource of a : a memory window, a port range or a RAM-backed window a driver asks the binding to map by index, or an unassigned slot () a bus keeps so the indices stay what its hardware numbers them. Architecture-neutral by construction: a window is a physical range whatever the architecture, and the kit maps it with the attributes the architecture needs.

files.Title: Cosmos.Kernel.HAL.DriverKit.Resources.DeviceResourceKind
files.Summary: The kind of a : what its base and length mean and how the kit maps it.

files.Title: Cosmos.Kernel.HAL.DriverKit.Resources.DmaBuffer
files.Summary: Physically contiguous, zeroed memory a device reads and writes directly, allocated through . The CPU sees it through , the device through . DMA is coherent on the machines the kernel runs on, so only ordering is needed: between filling a descriptor and the store that hands it over, between a flag the device wrote and the data it guards. A access carries its own barriers. Managed arrays are not DMA memory: the pinned heap is collected when nothing references an array, and a device holds no reference. is the same memory as a , for a display whose framebuffer is DMA memory.

files.Title: Cosmos.Kernel.HAL.DriverKit.Resources.DmaConstraints
files.Summary: What a device can address, for . The default asks for nothing beyond the alignment.

files.Title: Cosmos.Kernel.HAL.DriverKit.Resources.RegionCaching
files.Summary: How the CPU caches a bulk device region: the attribute the architecture applies to its accesses to it.

files.Title: Cosmos.Kernel.HAL.DriverKit.Resources.RegisterWindow
files.Summary: A window of device registers, mapped through . Each accessor is one access of its width, in program order, with the ordering the architecture needs: a write is preceded by a DMA write barrier, so the device sees every earlier store to DMA memory before the register write that tells it to look, and a read is followed by a DMA read barrier, so no later load from DMA memory runs ahead of the register that said the data is there. Over a memory window the accesses are device-memory loads and stores; over a port range on x64 they are in and out, and the same driver code works over either. Offsets are checked against the window's bounds, and over a memory window against the access width's alignment; ports are byte addressed, so a port range accepts any offset. The accessors neither allocate nor block, so an interrupt handler may use them.

files.Title: Cosmos.Kernel.HAL.DriverKit.Threading.DeviceEvent
files.Summary: A counted signal between a handler and a thread, created through . A handler signals it; a thread waits through , which is the only way to wait, so a handler holding the event cannot block on it. Teardown cancels it, and every waiter then returns false, at once and forever.

files.Title: Cosmos.Kernel.HAL.DriverKit.Threading.DeviceLock
files.Summary: A lock the kit sanctions for a driver whose device is entered from more than one context at once: a transmit path the ring calls from its own thread while the driver's work item, delivering a frame, re-enters it through the stack's synchronous reply; a handler and a thread sharing a register sequence. Created through ; it holds no resource, is not counted among them and needs no release. Any context: the holder runs with interrupts disabled, so a handler can never spin on a thread that holds it.

files.Title: Cosmos.Kernel.HAL.DriverKit.Threading.DeviceLockScope
files.Summary: The held state of a , returned by : a using binds to it, and releases the lock then restores the interrupt state the acquire found. Any context; disposed once, in the context that acquired. A default instance holds nothing and disposes to nothing.

files.Title: Cosmos.Kernel.HAL.DriverKit.Threading.DriverThread
files.Summary: A thread a driver started through . Its body loops on the binding's events until turns true, then returns; teardown joins it with a bounded wait.

files.Title: Cosmos.Kernel.HAL.DriverKit.Threading.WorkItem
files.Summary: A callback that runs in thread context on the kit worker, created through . Scheduling it from a handler is how interrupt work reaches a context that may block: the item is queued at most once at a time and allocation-free, because it owns its queue entry. Teardown cancels it; a cancelled item never runs again.

files.Title: Cosmos.Kernel.System.Audio.AudioDevice
files.Summary: One published audio output as the ring sees it: the name the driver gave it, which driver published it, where it sits in the device tree, and its format read live from the driver. Created by when the kit publishes an output and kept in 's list until it is withdrawn. Once withdrawn every call is a no-op and the format reads empty; the identity members are copied at creation, so they stay readable.

files.Title: Cosmos.Kernel.System.Audio.AudioManager
files.Summary: The audio outputs the kit published, and which one is primary. Every output a kit driver publishes is listed by the manager's from the kit worker and dropped when it is withdrawn. is the short way to put a stream through the primary output. Reads answer honestly before ran and when audio is compiled out: 0, null, false.

files.Title: Cosmos.Kernel.System.Audio.AudioPlayback
files.Summary:
An running on a thread of its own, so the caller gets on with its work while the audio plays. The thread wakes a few times per ring to top the device up and sleeps in between, which is why a kernel keeps its console, its timers and its drivers while a file plays.

Needs the scheduler running: without it there is no second thread to put this on and says so, leaving the caller to play the stream inline through .

The stream is read from the playback thread from here on. A stream over a filesystem is therefore read while the rest of the kernel runs, and the filesystem layer has no locking of its own: a caller that streams off a volume should leave that volume alone until the playback ends.

files.Title: Cosmos.Kernel.System.Audio.AudioPlaybackState
files.Summary: Where a background has got to.

files.Title: Cosmos.Kernel.System.Audio.AudioPlayer
files.Summary:
Pushes an into an until the stream runs out. The device owns the ring and drains it on the codec's clock; the player only keeps it fed, which is why it neither allocates per buffer nor runs from an interrupt.

Thread context: blocks for the length of the audio, and claims the output for as long as it runs, so two players cannot interleave frames into one ring. runs it on a thread of its own for a caller that must stay responsive; ends it early and is safe from any context.

files.Title: Cosmos.Kernel.System.Audio.AudioStream
files.Summary: A source of interleaved audio frames. The base class carries no length and no position on purpose: a stream may be endless, as a mixer or a capture device is. adds both for the finite ones.

files.Title: Cosmos.Kernel.System.Audio.MemoryAudioStream
files.Summary: A finite stream over frames already in memory, and the RIFF/WAVE reader that builds one from a .wav file. Only uncompressed LPCM is read, which is what a .wav almost always carries.

files.Title: Cosmos.Kernel.System.Audio.SeekableAudioStream
files.Summary: A finite audio stream whose position can be read and moved.

files.Title: Cosmos.Kernel.System.Audio.WaveAudioStream
files.Summary: A RIFF/WAVE stream read straight off a volume, a block at a time. The chunk list is walked over the file handle rather than over a buffer, so nothing larger than one chunk header is held to find the frames, and a file of any size plays in a fixed amount of memory. The handle stays open for the life of the stream and belongs to whoever opened it.

files.Title: Cosmos.Kernel.System.Audio.WaveHeader
files.Summary: What the reader needs out of a RIFF/WAVE file's chunk list: the frame layout, the rate, and where the frames themselves begin and end. A .wav is a chunk list rather than a fixed header, so the chunks between fmt and data are walked rather than assumed away: a file carrying a LIST or fact chunk reads like any other.

files.Title: Cosmos.Kernel.System.Diagnostics.DeviceNodeInfo
files.Summary:
Point-in-time snapshot of one device node in the driver kit's tree, produced by . The snapshot is taken without locking the kit, so a node whose offer or teardown is running on the kit worker may read one job stale: its state and the counts that depend on its binding can lag the log by one line.

It carries what a monitor can render off an unlocked read: identity, state, the driver that holds it, and counts. The offers themselves are reached by index through , bounded by ; and are counts only.

files.Title: Cosmos.Kernel.System.Diagnostics.DeviceNodeState
files.Summary: Where a device node is in its life, as reported by . A node enters the tree pending, is offered to the matching drivers once, ends up bound or unbound, and stays listed as retracted after its bus took it away.

files.Title: Cosmos.Kernel.System.Diagnostics.DeviceOfferInfo
files.Summary: One offer of a device node to a driver and how it ended, produced by . A node's offers are recorded in the order they were made, so walking them from index 0 replays the arbitration: which drivers were tried, in what order, and why each one passed. Offers are written once, when the node is offered, and never change afterwards.

files.Title: Cosmos.Kernel.System.Diagnostics.DeviceOfferOutcome
files.Summary: How one offer of a device node to a driver ended, as reported by .

files.Title: Cosmos.Kernel.System.Diagnostics.DriverDiagnostics
files.Summary:
Diagnostic view of the driver kit: whether the engine has started and how it runs, the driver manifest, the device tree with every offer made for each node, and the devices drivers have published. All reads are allocation-free and safe to poll from a monitor loop; the snapshot structs copy references out. Snapshots are taken without locking the kit, so a node or device whose offer, teardown or withdrawal is running on the kit worker may read one job stale.

Three shapes report "nothing there", and which one a member uses follows from what it is. A plain read answers with its own empty value, so and are false and and are 0 before the engine starts, with no separate error channel. and can be non-zero before then: the manifest registers its drivers ahead of the start, and a bus may publish nodes ahead of it, which sit pending until the start offers them. A read that must hand back a whole snapshot cannot express absence in the snapshot itself, so , , and are Try members and the bool carries that answer: false for an index out of range, which before the start is every device and offer index, while a driver or node index can already be valid then, as said above. is a method because it adds the counts up on every call rather than handing back a value the kit holds. Nothing here acts on the kit, so nothing throws.

files.Title: Cosmos.Kernel.System.Diagnostics.DriverInfo
files.Summary: One entry of the driver manifest, produced by . The index it was read at is its manifest position, which is the last arbitration key: when two drivers match a node with the same priority and the same specificity, the one earlier in the manifest is offered first.

files.Title: Cosmos.Kernel.System.Diagnostics.KernelThreadInfo
files.Summary:
Point-in-time snapshot of one kernel thread, produced by . The snapshot is taken without locking the scheduler, so fields of a thread that is being rescheduled concurrently may be one tick stale.

This is a projection of , the thread control block on the experimental scheduler seam, and it is narrower on purpose. It carries what a monitor can render off an unlocked read: identity, state, and two totals. It leaves behind the saved stack pointer, the entry address, the stack base and the two scheduling timestamps, because each of those is meaningful only in a state the snapshot cannot guarantee it is observing, and a policy that wants them already holds the control block. Two names differ from the seam's, both to state a unit the seam leaves to its own docs: and .

files.Title: Cosmos.Kernel.System.Diagnostics.KernelThreadState
files.Summary: Lifecycle state of a kernel thread as reported by .

files.Title: Cosmos.Kernel.System.Diagnostics.Log
files.Summary: Kernel debug log, written to the platform serial port (COM1 on x64, PL011 on ARM64). This is the supported way for kernels to emit debug output that a host can capture; on QEMU the stream appears on the -serial device. Writes are synchronous, allocation-free for strings and numbers, and usable from the earliest phase of BeforeRun onward.

files.Title: Cosmos.Kernel.System.Diagnostics.MemoryDiagnostics
files.Summary: Diagnostic view of the kernel's physical-memory and garbage-collector statistics, plus a forced collection. Every figure is a property, and each is a plain field read with no allocation, so they are safe to poll from a monitor loop at display refresh rate. The two collector counters are read independently rather than as a pair, so a collection landing between two reads shows up in one of them and not the other. Managed-heap figures beyond these counters come from the BCL ().

files.Title: Cosmos.Kernel.System.Diagnostics.PublishedDeviceInfo
files.Summary: Point-in-time snapshot of one device a driver published, produced by . A withdrawn device leaves the list, but the snapshot is taken without locking the kit, so a device being withdrawn concurrently may still be listed for one job; tells that case apart.

files.Title: Cosmos.Kernel.System.Diagnostics.PublishedDeviceKind
files.Summary: The kind of a device a driver published, as reported by . The set is closed: each kind is one contract a driver implements and one consumer slot the kernel's manager of that kind occupies.

files.Title: Cosmos.Kernel.System.Diagnostics.SchedulerDiagnostics
files.Summary:
Diagnostic view of the kernel scheduler: feature and lifecycle state, per-CPU thread tables, and the global thread registry, plus a request to terminate a thread by ID. All reads are allocation-free and safe to poll from a monitor loop; snapshots of threads that are being rescheduled concurrently may be one tick stale.

Three shapes report "nothing there", and which one a member uses follows from what it is. A plain read answers with its own empty value, so , , , , and are 0 and is null before the scheduler exists, with no separate error channel. A read that must hand back a whole snapshot cannot express absence in the snapshot itself, so it is a Try and the bool carries that answer. is the one member that acts rather than reads, and a bool would not tell a caller which of five things happened, so it returns ; that enum is its failure channel as well, and it reports rather than throwing when the scheduler is compiled out.

files.Summary: Outcome of .

files.Summary: A drawing surface: a buffer of raw ARGB pixels, either off-screen or attached to a display the driver kit published. Every primitive draws into the buffer; a display-backed canvas copies it to the display's framebuffer in , so it is double buffered and its pixels read back exactly as drawn. Subclassed by for a display that renders 3D.

Created by when the kit publishes a display and kept in 's list until it is withdrawn; a canvas holds one to draw on. files.Title: Cosmos.Kernel.System.Graphics.Fonts.TrueTypeFont
files.Summary: Represents a TrueType font. Unlike the fixed-cell bitmap fonts, glyphs have individual widths and pair kerning, and the font can be rasterized at any pixel size. holds the raw bytes of the .ttf file; and are zero because a TrueType font has no fixed character cell. Rasterized glyphs are cached per (character, size) as grayscale coverage, so the same font instance can draw in any color without re-rasterizing.

Decoding is done entirely in managed code by the vendored BigGustave decoder and SharpZipLib inflater (see the Credits page of the documentation).

files.Title: Cosmos.Kernel.System.Network.Protocols.EthernetPacket
files.Summary: An Ethernet frame, the root of the packet hierarchy. The frame lives in ; every header property is a snapshot parsed from that buffer at construction time and is not refreshed by later writes to the buffer. Derived types lay their headers into the same buffer from their constructors, including checksums: there is no separate finalize-before-send step.

files.Title: Cosmos.Kernel.System.Network.Protocols.IPv4.Dhcp.DhcpDiscover

files.Title: Cosmos.Kernel.System.Network.Protocols.IPv4.Dhcp.DhcpRelease

files.Title: Cosmos.Kernel.System.Network.Protocols.IPv4.Dhcp.DhcpRequest

files.Title: Cosmos.Kernel.System.Network.Protocols.IPv4.IPPacket
files.Summary: An IPv4 packet over Ethernet. The build constructors write the complete IPv4 header, including the header checksum, at construction time; the checksum is never recomputed, so the header bytes must not be modified afterwards. Derive from this class to implement a custom IP protocol that only IPv4 carries: pass the protocol number and payload length to a build constructor and write the payload into from onward. A protocol that both versions carry composes an instead of deriving from this class, the way and do.

files.Title: Cosmos.Kernel.System.Network.Protocols.IPv4.IcmpEchoReply
files.Summary: An ICMP echo reply packet. The identifier and sequence properties are snapshots parsed from at construction time.

files.Title: Cosmos.Kernel.System.Network.Protocols.IPv4.IcmpEchoRequest
files.Summary: An ICMP echo request packet. The identifier and sequence properties are snapshots parsed from at construction time.

files.Title: Cosmos.Kernel.System.Network.Protocols.IPv4.IcmpPacket
files.Summary: An ICMP packet carried in an (IP protocol 1). Header properties are snapshots parsed from at construction time; the checksum is computed in the constructors and never recomputed afterward.

files.Title: Cosmos.Kernel.System.Network.Protocols.InternetPacket
files.Summary: The internet layer of a frame: an IPv4 or an IPv6 packet. A transport protocol composes one of these instead of deriving from it, which is what lets a single transport class serve both versions: the internet packet owns the frame buffer, reports where the transport section starts and how long it is, computes the transport checksum with its own pseudo-header, and queues itself on the outgoing buffer that resolves its kind of neighbor address.

files.Title: Cosmos.Kernel.System.Network.Protocols.Tcp.TcpFlags
files.Summary: TCP header control flags, as defined by RFC 793.

files.Title: Cosmos.Kernel.System.Network.Protocols.Tcp.TcpOption
files.Summary: A TCP header option parsed from a received segment. Options are parse products only: the stack reads them from incoming segments but never serializes them into packets it builds.

files.Title: Cosmos.Kernel.System.Network.Protocols.Tcp.TcpPacket
files.Summary: A TCP segment, over IPv4 or over IPv6. The wire header is the same on both, so one class serves both: the segment composes the that carries it rather than deriving from a version-specific packet, and reads the frame buffer, the addresses and the segment offset back through . The one part that differs by version is the checksum pseudo-header, which the internet packet supplies.

files.Title: Cosmos.Kernel.System.Network.Protocols.Udp.UdpPacket
files.Summary: A UDP datagram, over IPv4 or over IPv6. The wire header is the same on both, so one class serves both: the datagram composes the that carries it rather than deriving from a version-specific packet, and reads the frame buffer, the addresses and the payload offset back through .

files.Title: Cosmos.Kernel.System.Power

files.Title: Cosmos.Kernel.System.Sessions.ConsoleSession
files.Summary: One console that can be bound to: a screen, and the keys typed at it. The local virtual consoles and the connections of a remote terminal server, such as the Cosmos.Network.Telnet package's, are all sessions. numbers them, shows one of them on the display, and binds every thread to one, so the same calls read and write whichever session the calling thread belongs to.

files.Title: Cosmos.Kernel.System.Sessions.SessionManager
files.Summary: Keeps the console sessions: numbers them, shows one on the display, and binds each thread to one, which is what reads and writes on that thread.

files.Title: Cosmos.Kernel.System.Storage.Ebr
files.Summary:
EBR (Extended Boot Record) chain parser and editor. An extended partition contains a singly-linked list of EBR sectors; each EBR holds one logical partition entry plus an optional pointer to the next EBR. Convention used:

  • Logical-entry start LBA is relative to the EBR sector that holds it.
  • Next-EBR pointer is relative to the extended partition's start LBA (the standard convention).
  • The first EBR always sits at the extended partition's start LBA.
  • Each subsequent EBR is placed immediately after the prior logical's data.

files.Title: Cosmos.Kernel.System.Storage.Gpt
files.Summary: GPT (GUID Partition Table) parser / writer. Reads / writes the primary header at LBA 1 plus the partition entry array starting at LBA 2. 512-byte sectors assumed (matches every block device this kernel currently exposes).

files.Title: Cosmos.Kernel.System.Storage.GptPartitionEntry
files.Summary: Single parsed partition. Sector positions are absolute on the host disk.

files.Title: Cosmos.Kernel.System.Storage.Mbr
files.Summary: MBR (Master Boot Record) partition table parser / writer. Operates on any with 512-byte sectors.

files.Title: Cosmos.Kernel.System.Storage.MbrPartitionEntry
files.Summary: Single MBR partition entry. Sector positions are absolute on the host disk.

files.Title: Cosmos.Kernel.System.Storage.Partition
files.Summary: Block-device view of a single partition on a host disk. Read/Write are translated to the host LBA space by adding .

files.Title: Cosmos.Kernel.System.Storage.PartitionManager.PartitionLocation
files.Summary: Identifies a partition by its absolute LBA range on the host disk.

files.Title: Cosmos.Kernel.System.Storage.PartitionManager
files.Summary: High-level partition lifecycle (create / delete / resize / move) on top of and . Auto-detects the table type per call. physically copies sectors before rewriting the table; the other operations are pure table edits.

files.Title: Cosmos.Kernel.System.Storage.StorageManager
files.Summary:
Manages block storage devices. A disk reaches the manager one of two ways: a driver kit driver publishes it and the manager's registers it (the AHCI, NVMe, virtio-blk and USB mass storage drivers), or it is handed to directly by the kernel. Every registration scans the disk for partitions. The tables change after boot too, when a USB disk, or a virtio-blk disk behind a PCI Express hot-plug slot, is plugged in or pulled out, from the kit worker in a probe or a teardown: each is replaced whole on every change, so a list read from , or never changes under its reader. Read it once and index that copy: a second read may be a newer table.

The tables are kept in one order, which decides the primary device: a kit disk before a hand-registered one; among kit disks the smaller node path by ordinal comparison (pci: before usb: before virtio:), and among equal paths the earlier registered; among hand-registered disks the earlier registered. So an internal disk on a PCI controller comes before a USB stick present at boot whichever registered first, and a kit disk arriving after a USB stick moves ahead of it and renumbers , which is why a mount by keeps its partition where a mount by index string keeps its index.

files.Title: Cosmos.Kernel.System.Timers.AlarmManager
files.Summary:
Runs callbacks after a delay on a dedicated kernel thread. Alarm callbacks run in thread context, so they may block, allocate and use scheduler primitives, unlike the interrupt-context callbacks of . Requires the scheduler; resolution is bounded by the scheduler tick.

The scheduling calls themselves also run in thread context only. Every member here takes the alarm list's mutex and parks if it is held, so calling one from an interrupt handler, a callback included, parks inside the handler and hangs. The members mask interrupts instead of parking and have no such restriction.

files.Title: Cosmos.Kernel.System.Timers.SoftwareTimer
files.Summary: A software timer that invokes a callback after a delay, driven by the periodic tick of the platform tick source. Callbacks run in interrupt context: they must not block, and an exception escaping one halts the kernel, because the interrupt dispatch has no handler above it.

files.Title: Cosmos.Kernel.System.Timers.TimerManager
files.Summary: Manages system timers.
